A trip through time

  1. Triassic

    252 to 201 million years ago

    The first dinosaurs appear, about 230 million years ago. Many are small and run on two legs.

  2. Jurassic

    201 to 145 million years ago

    Giant plant-eaters like Brontosaurus and Stegosaurus. The first birds fly.

  3. Cretaceous

    145 to 66 million years ago

    T. rex, Triceratops and the first flowers. It ends when a huge asteroid hits Earth.

  4. Today

    66 million years ago to now

    The big dinosaurs are gone, but birds are still here. They are dinosaurs too!

Questions

Are the bones real?

Some are real fossils: bones that turned to stone. The biggest skeletons are copies, so the real bones stay safe.

Can I touch anything?

Yes! Look for the hand sign. At those tables you can touch fossil teeth and shells.

Did people live with dinosaurs?

No. The big dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago. The first people came millions of years later.

Is there a cafe?

Yes, right next to the T. rex hall. T. rex would have trouble holding the spoon.

Nova Newt
  • Coin hunt
  • Pick a door
  • How it works

How it works

Is this a real game, or just a website? It is both! There is no JavaScript here, only HTML and CSS. These are the tricks, with the important lines from style.css.

A label clicks its checkbox

Every coin is a checkbox. The box itself is hidden. What you see is its label, drawn to look like a coin. When you click a label, the browser clicks its checkbox for you. They belong together because for="coin-1" and id="coin-1" match.

<input class="coin-box" type="checkbox" id="coin-1">
<label class="coin" for="coin-1">
  <span class="hidden-text">Coin 1</span>
</label>

Try it here. This checkbox is not hidden, so you can watch it:

:checked changes the look

:checked means "this checkbox has a tick". The + means "the label right after it". So when a coin box gets a tick, its coin fades away, and the mouse can not click it again. In style.css the coin also does a little jump first.

.coin-box:checked + .coin {
  opacity: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
}

counter-increment counts

CSS can count! counter-reset starts a counter at 0. Every box with a tick adds 1. Then content writes the number on the screen.

.game { counter-reset: coins; }
.coin-box:checked { counter-increment: coins; }
.score::before {
  content: "Coins: " counter(coins) " of 8";
}

CSS counts from the top of the page to the bottom. That is why the score comes after all 8 coins in index.html.

:has() and :target ask questions

:has() looks inside a box. This rule asks: "Does the game have a coin box with no tick?" :not() turns the question around. When no coin is left, the Level clear banner shows.

.game:not(:has(.coin-box:not(:checked))) .level-clear {
  display: grid;
}

:target is the part of the page whose id is at the end of the address. The doors are links like href="#door-2". Click one, and the box with id="door-2" becomes the target, so it shows.

.result { display: none; }
.result:target { display: grid; }

Do real game sites work like this?

Not often. Most games on the web use JavaScript, a programming language that runs in the browser. It can move a hero with the arrow keys, play sounds and save your best score. This site has no JavaScript. It shows how far HTML and CSS can go on their own.

Try it yourself:

  • Move a coin: change left and top in .spot-1 in style.css.
  • Paint the coins: change --coin in :root.
  • Add a 9th coin: copy a coin in index.html and change its numbers to 9. Add a .spot-9 place in style.css, and change "of 8" to "of 9". Then change the 8 at the top of index.html and in the Level clear words.

Build a Scribble Bot

A shaking cup on felt-tip pen legs that draws all by itself. It takes about 45 minutes. You need a grown-up for step 6.

You need

Not sure what a part is? Look in the parts box

Get your parts

Put all the parts on the table. Tick each one off in the list when you find it.

Give the cup legs

Turn the cup upside down. Tape three pens round the edge, tips down, caps on. Now the cup stands on its pens.

Make a wobble weight

Push the cork onto the motor shaft, near its edge and not in the middle. Now one side is heavier.

Why does it wobble?

When the motor spins, the heavy side of the cork pulls this way, then that way, very fast. That shakes the whole robot.

Some phones buzz the same way: inside is a tiny motor with a weight that is not in the middle.

Put the motor on top

Tape the motor flat on top of the cup. The cork sticks out past the edge, so it can spin round freely.

Add the battery holder

Tape the battery holder to the side of the cup. Keep the batteries out for now.

Connect the wires

Join the red wire of the motor to the red wire of the holder. Then join black to black. Twist the ends together and tape them.

Ask a grown-up to help with this step.

Give it a face

Stick on the googly eyes. Now your robot can see! (No, it can't. But it looks like it can.)

Let it draw

Take the caps off the pens. Put the batteries in and set your robot on a big sheet of paper. Watch it shake and scribble!

Does it only spin on the spot? Move the cork a little, or bend one pen leg out.

Our mission story

First our ship swings around the Moon. Then it zooms to Mars, the red planet. After that comes the long ride to giant Jupiter, and to Saturn with its shiny rings.

A grid is a net of lines, and you put boxes between the lines. Every grid on this page has hidden lines. Flip the switch to see them: each line runs along the gap between two dashed boxes.

Meet Big Bert, the pumpkin that took over the school garden

One seed, one sunny corner and a lot of watering cans. This is how the garden club grew the biggest pumpkin our school has ever seen.

By Noor and Sami, class 5. A 3-minute read.

One flat, white seed started it all. In May, the garden club planted it in a pot on the classroom window. About ten days later, two round leaves pushed up through the soil.

In June the little plant moved outside, into the sunny corner by the fence. "We gave it lots of compost," says Sami. "Pumpkins are very hungry plants."

By July the plant had big, rough leaves and long vines. Bright yellow flowers opened in the mornings. Bees flew from flower to flower, and soon a tiny green pumpkin started to grow behind one of the flowers.

That tiny pumpkin was Big Bert.

In August Bert grew so fast that we measured him every morning before lessons.

Noor, class 5

The garden club put straw under Bert, so he stayed dry and clean. They turned the vines away from the football pitch. They even made a little sign: Please do not sit on Bert.

In late September Bert turned deep orange, and his stalk went hard and woody. That is how gardeners know a pumpkin is ripe. Mr Ashdown cut the stalk with big garden scissors, and four pupils rolled Bert onto a wheelbarrow.

On the school kitchen scales, Bert weighed 38 kilograms. That is about as heavy as a big dog.

So what happens now? The school kitchen will turn Bert into soup for everyone. The garden club will save his seeds, and next May they plan to grow Big Bert's little brother.

Pumpkin facts

  • A pumpkin is a fruit, because it grows from a flower and has seeds inside.
  • Pumpkins grow on long vines that creep along the ground.
  • A pumpkin is a kind of squash.
  • Pumpkin flowers are bright yellow, and bees carry pollen between them.

How we build a bike

6 steps, 1 bike

The bike line

Every bike goes along the line step by step. Follow the red arrows!

  1. Cut the tubes

    Long metal tubes are cut to the right length for the frame.

  2. Weld the frame

    Welding melts the metal at the joins, so the tubes become one strong frame.

  3. Paint it

    Colour powder is sprayed on. Then an oven bakes it into a hard, shiny coat.

  4. Build the wheels

    Thin spokes join the hub in the middle to the rim on the outside.

  5. Put it together

    Wheels, chain, pedals, brakes, saddle and bell go on the frame.

  6. Test ride

    A tester rides every bike and checks the brakes twice. Ready!

Why so many spokes?

A bike wheel is mostly empty space! The thin spokes pull the rim in from all sides, so they share the weight of the rider. Many wheels have 32 or 36 spokes.

We check every wheel on a truing stand, a machine that shows where it wobbles, before it goes on a bike.

Brickbee Builders
  • Home

How we build a house

Eight big steps, one after the other. Most of them must wait for the step before.

The eight steps

  1. Plan and draw

    Weeks 1 to 8

    An architect draws every room. The town checks the plan and says yes.

  2. Clear and dig

    Week 9

    Diggers clear the ground and dig deep holes for the foundation.

  3. Pour the foundation

    Week 10

    Wet concrete fills the holes. It sets hard and holds the whole house up.

  4. Build the frame and walls

    Weeks 11 to 16

    The walls go up. Now you can walk through the rooms.

  5. Put on the roof

    Weeks 17 to 19

    The roof keeps the rain out, so the inside can stay dry.

  6. Pipes and wires

    Weeks 20 to 24

    Plumbers fit the water pipes. Electricians pull the wires for lights and plugs.

  7. Floors, walls and paint

    Weeks 25 to 32

    Floors go in, walls get smooth, and the painters add colour.

  8. Hand over the keys

    Week 33

    We check everything twice, tidy up and give the keys to the new family.

Site rules

  • Hard hat on, all the time.
  • Safety boots with steel toes.
  • A bright vest, so drivers can see you.
  • Never walk under a crane's load.
  • Visitors sign in at the site office.
  • Keep the site tidy. Tidy sites are safe sites.

Questions kids ask us

Why do cranes have big concrete blocks?

They are counterweights. The blocks sit on the short arm and balance the heavy load on the long arm, like a seesaw. Without them the crane would tip over.

What is a foundation?

It is the strong base under a house, mostly made of concrete. It spreads the weight of the house into the ground, so the house does not sink.

Why do builders wear bright vests?

Bright colours and shiny stripes are easy to see, even in rain or at dusk. Drivers and crane operators can spot every person on the site.

Why do builders test concrete after 28 days?

Concrete keeps getting harder for weeks, even months. After about a week it is strong enough to build on. Builders test a sample at 28 days to check it is as strong as the plan says.

How do bricks get so hard?

Bricks are made of clay. They are baked in a very hot oven called a kiln, at about 1000 degrees Celsius. The heat turns soft clay into something as hard as rock.

Can I visit a building site?

Not on your own: a building site is dangerous. Once a year we hold an open day, with small hard hats for kids and a ride in the digger seat.

Every box finds its way

At the Port of Brindlewick, big ships meet trucks and trains. Our cranes lift boxes day and night, all year round.

Track a ship See how a box moves

The box that changed the world

Toys, bikes and shoes in your home came across the sea in a steel box. Every box has the same strong corners, so cranes, ships, trucks and trains all over the world can carry it.

Ports count boxes in TEU. That means "twenty-foot equivalent unit": one short box. A long 40-foot box counts as 2 TEU.

Every box has its own code, painted on its door:

BRWU 204613 3

In this pretend code, three letters say who owns it. U means it is a box for goods. Then come six numbers, and the last number is a check number. It catches typing mistakes.

A port that never sleeps

Each ship ties up at a berth, its parking place at the quay. Ships cost a lot of money for every hour they wait, so we work in three shifts. When one team goes home, the next team climbs into the cranes.

How a box moves

From the moment the ship arrives to the truck at the gate, there are six stops. Here is every one.

Six stops from ship to truck

Swipe sideways to see all six stops.

  1. Pilot and tugs

    A harbour pilot climbs aboard and guides the ship in. Strong little tugboats push it to its berth, its parking place at the quay.

  2. Ropes on bollards

    Thick ropes go from the ship to iron bollards on the quay, the stone edge of the harbour, so the ship cannot drift away.

  3. Crane and spreader

    The crane lowers its spreader, a steel frame that grabs a box, onto the box. Twistlocks, small turning locks, turn in the four corners and hold on tight.

  4. Straddle carrier

    A straddle carrier, a tall truck on long legs, drives right over the box, picks it up and takes it to the yard.

  5. Yard stack

    Boxes wait in long stacks. A computer remembers each box code and the exact spot of the box.

  6. Customs and gate

    Customs officers check what is inside and check the papers. At the gate a truck picks up the box and drives it away.

How do boxes hold on?

Every box has a strong steel corner with an oval hole. A twistlock fits into the hole and turns a quarter of the way round. Now the boxes are locked together, so they stay in place when the ship rolls.

From wind to your plug

Electricity takes a long trip before it reaches your home. Here is every stop on the way.

The journey of electricity

Follow the arrows, from a puff of wind to the plug in your wall.

  1. Wind

    The wind pushes the three blades round and round.

  2. Generator

    The blades turn a shaft. Magnets spin past copper wire, and that makes electricity.

  3. Transformer

    It pushes the electricity much harder (that push is called voltage), so less of it is lost on the long trip.

  4. Power lines

    Tall towers carry the wires across the fields to the towns.

  5. Your plug

    A substation, a small fenced building full of machines, makes the push gentle again. Wires under the street bring it home.

And the sun?

Solar panels have no blades and no generator. The light does all the work.

  1. Sunlight

    Light from the sun reaches Earth in about 8 minutes.

  2. Solar panel

    Solar cells, mostly made of silicon, turn the light into electricity.

  3. Inverter

    The panel makes electricity that flows one way. The inverter changes it so it swings back and forth, like the electricity in your wall.

  4. Your home

    On a sunny day, lamps and fridges run on sunshine.

Did you know?

Before the blades start, the turbine turns its whole head to face the wind. A small wind vane on top tells it where the wind is coming from.

Raspberry chia jars

A pudding that makes itself while you sleep. You shake, you wait, you eat.

  • 10 minutes to make
  • Waits all night
  • Makes 2 jars
  • No knife, no oven

From Granny Edda's notebook, page 12

You need

Tick each one when it is on the table.

Tools

  • 2 jars with lids
  • A tablespoon and a teaspoon
  • A measuring jug

Steps

  1. Wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds.
  2. Put 2 tablespoons of chia seeds into each jar.
  3. Pour half of the milk into each jar. Add 1 teaspoon of honey and a drop of vanilla to each one.
  4. Close the lids tight. Shake each jar for 10 seconds.
  5. Wait 10 minutes, then shake again. This stops lumps.
  6. Put the jars in the fridge for at least 4 hours, or all night.
  7. Put the raspberries on top and eat it with a spoon!

Granny Edda's tip

Too thick? Stir in a splash of milk. Too runny? Put it back in the fridge for one more hour.

Why does it get thick?

Chia seeds drink. A dry seed can soak up about 12 times its own weight in liquid, and it grows a soft jelly coat. All those jelly coats together turn the milk into pudding.

Kitchen rules

Good cooks are safe cooks. Read these with an adult before your first recipe.

Seven rules for little chefs

  • Wash your hands. Use soap and scrub for 20 seconds. That is about as long as singing "Happy Birthday" twice.

  • Tie back long hair and roll up your sleeves, so nothing dips into the food.

  • Ask an adult first before you use the oven, the hob (the hot top of the cooker), a knife, the grater, the blender or the kettle.

  • Turn pan handles in, away from the front of the cooker, so nobody knocks a pan over.

  • Hot things need oven gloves, and an adult right next to you.

  • Wipe up spills straight away, so nobody slips.

  • Wash fruit and vegetables under running water before you eat them.

From sketch to shop

How does a doodle turn into a T-shirt you can wear? Follow the six steps, from the first pencil line to the shop.

  1. 01

    Sketch

    Every T-shirt starts with a pencil. We draw lots of ideas, and kids send us their doodles too. Most ideas stay on paper. Only the best one moves on.

  2. 02

    Pick the colours

    We choose three or four colours that look good together. A colour wheel helps. Colours on opposite sides of the wheel make each other look brighter.

  3. 03

    Make a pattern

    A pattern is a small picture that repeats, like tiles on a wall. Look in style.css: one small circle, repeated, makes all the polka dots.

  4. 04

    Cut the fabric

    Paper shapes are laid on the fabric, and we cut around them. A T-shirt has a front, a back, two sleeves and a thin strip for the neck.

  5. 05

    Sew it together

    A sewing machine joins the pieces. T-shirt fabric stretches, so the stitches must stretch too. A zig-zag stitch can stretch without breaking.

  6. 06

    Off to the shop

    Last, every T-shirt is checked and folded. A small label inside tells the size and how to wash it. Then it is ready for you!

Favourite animal

I take photos of nature: animals, plants, mountains and the sky. I started when I was nine, with an old camera from my grandma.

What is in my bag

  • A camera with a long lens, to see shy animals from far away
  • A tripod with three legs, to hold the camera still
  • A rain cover, because forests are wet
  • Gloves with open fingertips, for pressing buttons in the cold
  • A notebook, to write down what I saw
  • Snacks. Waiting makes you hungry!

How I take a photo

  1. Be quiet and wait

    Animals hide when they hear you. Sit still and let them come.

  2. Look at the light

    Soft morning light makes colours glow. Midday sun makes hard shadows.

  3. Get down low

    Hold the camera at the animal's eye level, not above it.

  4. Keep the horizon straight

    A tilted sea looks like it is spilling out of the photo.

  5. Take many, keep one

    Take lots of photos. At home, pick the very best one.

A big, furry bee. It shivers its flying muscles to warm up, so it can fly on cool days.

Where and when: flowers, March to October

It tastes with its feet! It drinks nectar through a long tongue that curls up like a spring when it is not in use.

Dragonfly

It catches other insects in the air, and it can even fly backwards. A young dragonfly lives underwater, often for a year or two, before it gets its wings.

Where and when: ponds and rivers, May to September

Earwig

The pincers at its back end can only give a weak pinch. Earwig mothers guard their eggs all winter and keep them clean. And earwigs almost never go near ears. That story is a myth!

Where and when: under bark and flower pots, spring to autumn

A ladybird is a small beetle. Its bright spots warn birds that it tastes horrible. It eats greenfly, tiny bugs that suck the juice out of plants.

Many moths fly at night and rest in the day. Moths often have feathery or thin antennae. A butterfly has a little club on the end of each one.

What makes an insect?

Every insect has three body parts and six legs. Look at the drawing, then hide the labels and test yourself.

Head
The front part. It holds the eyes, the antennae and the mouth.
Antennae
Two feelers on the head. Insects use them to smell and to touch.
Eyes
Big eyes made of many tiny parts. A dragonfly's eye has thousands of them.
Thorax
The middle part. All six legs and all the wings join on here.
Six legs
Three pairs, all on the thorax. Every grown-up insect has six.
Wings
Most grown-up insects have four. Flies have two, and worker ants have none.
Abdomen
The back part, with the stomach inside. A bee's or a wasp's sting is at the very end.
Exoskeleton
An insect has no bones. Its hard skin is its skeleton, on the outside!

Insect or not?

Count the legs and the body parts, then open each one to check.

A spider?

A spider has eight legs and only two body parts, so it is not an insect.

A woodlouse?

A woodlouse has 14 legs, so it is not an insect. It is a cousin of crabs and shrimps.

A centipede?

A centipede has far more than six legs, so it is not an insect. Funny thing: it never has exactly 100.

A ladybird?

Yes, a ladybird is an insect, with six legs, three body parts and four wings. The front two wings are its hard red cases.

Go insect spotting

The best insect spotters are slow, quiet and gentle. Here is where to look, and how to look without hurting anything.

Where to look

Under a log

Ants, earwigs and beetles hide where it is dark and damp.

On flowers

Bees, hoverflies and butterflies come to drink nectar.

By a pond

Pond skaters stand on the water. Dragonflies zoom above it.

In long grass

Listen for singing grasshoppers. Look for ladybirds on the stems.

Look, don't harm

  • Move slowly. Fast hands and a sudden shadow scare insects away.
  • Look, don't grab. For a closer look, let an insect walk onto a leaf.
  • Use a bug pot. A clear pot with air holes. Put the insect back where you found it after a few minutes.
  • Put logs back. Roll logs and stones back gently, the same way up, so the homes under them stay safe.
  • Wash your hands when you are done.

Never pick up stinging insects

Bees, wasps and hornets can sting. Watch them from a step away, and never put one in a bug pot.

If one flies close to you, stay calm and walk slowly away. Do not wave your arms.

How clouds are made

Every cloud starts as water on the ground. The sun does most of the work. Here is the trip a drop of water takes.

From puddle to cloud

  1. The sun warms water

    Seas, lakes and puddles get warm. Some water turns into a gas you cannot see, called water vapour. This is evaporation.

  2. Warm air rises

    Warm air goes up and carries the vapour with it. The higher it goes, the colder the air gets.

  3. Tiny drops appear

    In cold air the vapour turns back into tiny drops around specks of dust, salt or smoke. This is condensation. Billions of drops make a cloud.

  4. Rain falls

    The drops bump together and grow. When they are too heavy to float, they fall as rain, or as snow when it is cold enough.

Four clouds to spot

The tools on our roof

ToolWhat it measures
ThermometerHow warm or cold the air is
Rain gaugeHow much rain has fallen
AnemometerHow fast the wind blows
Wind vaneWhere the wind comes from
BarometerHow hard the air presses down
HygrometerHow full of water vapour the air is

Cloud quiz

Think of your answer first, then click the question to check.

What is a cloud made of?

Billions of tiny drops of water, or tiny bits of ice, floating in the air.

Water is heavy. Why does a cloud not fall down?

Cloud drops are much smaller than rain drops. They are so light that rising air holds them up.

Which cloud brings thunder and lightning?

The cumulonimbus, the tall storm cloud.

What is fog?

A stratus cloud that sits on the ground. Walking in fog is walking inside a cloud!

Why do rain clouds look grey?

They are thick and full of water, so less sunlight gets through them. From below, they look dark.

Three shapes of volcano

The lava decides the shape. Runny lava spreads out into wide, gentle volcanoes. Sticky lava, ash and lumps of lava pile up into steep ones. Point at a card, or press Tab, to fill it with lava.

Shield volcano

Wide and gentle

  • Runny lava flows a long way before it cools, so the sides are low and wide.
  • Mauna Loa in Hawaii is a shield volcano. It is the biggest active volcano on Earth.

Cinder cone

Small and steep

  • Lumps of lava fly out of one vent, cool in the air and pile up into a steep hill.
  • Parícutin in Mexico started in a farmer's cornfield in 1943.

Stratovolcano

Tall and steep

  • It is built from many layers of hardened lava and ash, one on top of another.
  • Mount Fuji in Japan is a stratovolcano. So is our Mount Cinderkettle!

Which volcano is it?

A small, steep hill with a bowl on top, made of lava lumps?

A cinder cone. The lumps landed all around the vent, like sand in an egg timer.

So wide and low, it looks like a shield lying on the ground?

A shield volcano. That look is where its name comes from.

Tall and steep, with stripes of lava and ash inside?

A stratovolcano. "Strata" means layers. Look for the stripes in our drawing on the first page.

How we keep watch

A volcano often gives signs before it erupts. We measure them every day, so people who live nearby can get ready in time.

What we measure

Ground shaking

Rising magma cracks the rock and makes small earthquakes. A seismometer feels shakes that are too small for people to notice.

Gas

Magma lets out gases, such as sulfur dioxide. If more gas comes out each day, magma may be moving up. Our gas sensors measure it.

Swelling

Magma pushing up can make the ground bulge, like a balloon under a carpet. GPS stations and tiltmeters (machines that feel the ground tip a tiny bit) notice even a tiny bulge.

Our alert colours

Real volcano observatories use colours like these to tell pilots how the volcano is doing.

  1. Green Quiet. A normal day.
  2. Yellow Restless. More shakes or gas than usual.
  3. Orange Very restless, or a small eruption has started.
  4. Red A big eruption with lots of ash is close or happening.

Volcano words

Magma
Melted rock under the ground.
Lava
Magma that has come out on top of the ground.
Ash
Tiny pieces of rock and glass thrown out by a volcano.
Eruption
When lava, ash or gas comes out of a volcano.
Active
Erupting now, or it erupted in about the last 10,000 years. For a volcano, that is not long ago!
Dormant
Sleeping. It has not erupted for a long time, but it could wake up.
Extinct
Finished. It is not expected to erupt ever again.
Seismometer
A machine that feels the ground shaking.
Volcanologist
A scientist who studies volcanoes.

Visiting a volcano park?

  • Stay on the marked paths. The ground near a vent can be thin and hot.
  • Read the signs and listen to the park rangers.
  • Keep away from steam and gas holes. Some volcano gases are bad to breathe.

Real volcano scientists share their news here: USGS Volcano Hazards Program

A house in six boxes

Here is the little house again, built one shape at a time. Each step adds one box. The new box is in colour, the old ones turn grey.

  1. 1. The wall A box with a background colour.

  2. 2. The roof clip-path cuts a box into a triangle.

  3. 3. The door border-radius rounds the top corners.

  4. 4. The window Two linear-gradient stripes make the cross.

How to cut a triangle

clip-path: polygon() joins dots and cuts away the rest. Each dot is two numbers: how far across, then how far down the box.

The roof has class="house-roof tri". Its cut lives in the class tri, so every triangle can share it:

.tri {
  clip-path: polygon(50% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100%);
}
50% 0 100% 100% 0 100%

One house, three sizes

Every size in the house is in em. One em is as big as the font-size. So when the font-size grows, the whole house grows with it.

This page is a mountain trail. Scroll down slowly: each yellow sign stops at the top of the window and waits, and the next sign stacks under it, like the arrows on a signpost.

The trick is position: sticky. Find the block called STICKY SIGNS in style.css.

Village 1200 m

The trail starts at the fountain in the village square. Fill your water bottle here: there is no shop until the hut at the top.

Pine forest 1500 m

The path climbs in zigzags under tall pine trees. It is cool and shady, and it smells of resin. Count the pine cones on the path.

Flower meadow 1900 m

Above the trees, the meadow is full of tiny flowers. Listen for a sharp whistle: marmots whistle to warn their family when someone is coming.

Rocks and snow 2400 m

Now the path is made of rocks, and some snow stays all summer. Put on a jumper: on average the air gets about 6.5 degrees colder for every 1000 metres you climb.

Far things move slowly

Look out of a car window. The fence by the road zooms past. The trees further away go slower. The mountains far away hardly move at all. This is called parallax.

A mountain in five layers

Scroll inside this window. The trees move at full speed, the hills slower, the far peaks slower still, the sun slowest of all, and the sky not at all.

Scroll down inside me

  • Sky background does not move
  • Sun translateZ(-3px) scale(4) one quarter speed
  • Far peaks translateZ(-2px) scale(3) one third speed
  • Near hills translateZ(-1px) scale(2) half speed
  • Front trees transform: none full speed

translateZ pushes a layer away from you, deeper into the screen. Far away things look smaller, so scale makes the layer big again. Now it looks the same, but it scrolls slower. The window needs perspective: 1px to make the screen deep.

A hole in the page

Now scroll the whole page and watch the band below. The photo stays still and the band slides over it.

The band is a hole in the page. The cloud photo behind it is pinned to the window with background-attachment: fixed.

If the layers do not move

Some people feel sick when things on the screen slide at different speeds. They can ask their computer for less motion. Then this page shows the mountain flat, and the photo scrolls with the band. The CSS checks with prefers-reduced-motion.

Outline letters

Hollow

-webkit-text-stroke draws the edge, color: transparent empties the inside. Point at it to pour in red ink.

Writing downwards

TOWER

This line runs from the top down.

writing-mode: vertical-rl turns the line. text-orientation: upright stands each letter up. Japanese and Chinese can be written like this, in columns from right to left.

Letters in 3D

POP!

Eight text-shadow copies, each 1px further. Point at it to press it flat.

Letters that breathe

SPACE

letter-spacing puts air between the letters. Point at it.

A drop cap

Long ago, books were written by hand. The first letter of a chapter was often painted big and bright, in red or even in gold. When printing began, printers left an empty space, and a painter added that letter by hand.

::first-letter picks the first letter. float: left lets the lines flow round it.

Highlighter pen

A yellow pen marks the words that matter. This one even goes over two lines of text, and each line gets its own piece of yellow.

The yellow is a linear-gradient. Point at it: it grows from 0% to 100% wide.

Press, cut, underline

Four bigger tricks. Point at a box, or press Tab, and the pressed letters, the short story and the marble letters play.

Pressed into paper

Printed

A printing press pushes inked metal letters into the paper. On thick card it can leave a dent. Two text-shadows copy the dent: a dark edge 1px up and a light edge 1px down. Point at it to press harder.

Fancy underlines

wavy double thick

text-decoration-style makes the line wavy or double. text-decoration-thickness makes it fat, and text-underline-offset moves it down.

Text cut short

Once upon a time, a small metal letter A lived in a wooden box with all the other letters. Every morning the printer picked it up, put it in a line with its friends and pressed them onto paper. By the end of the day, the letter A had been in a hundred words: apple, cat, banana and many more.

-webkit-line-clamp: 3 stops the text after 3 lines and puts ... at the end. Shops and news sites use it for "read more" boxes. Point at it to read it all.

Letters cut from a picture

MARBLE

background-clip: text cuts the picture to the shape of the letters. The picture is marbled paper from France, about 1880: paint floats on water, and a sheet of paper picks it up. Point at it and the paper slides.
